text: Data Cleaning & Scope This exploratory analysis assesses the coverage of the CAT ratings against the full UBCBG IrisBG living collection. Additionally a taxonomic backbone from the World Online Flora was added to discuss some specific challenges of conservation. * Inclusion Criteria: All taxa that have been historically grown at the current UBC Botanical Garden (1970 -2024), taxa with full genera an specific epithet available in IrisBG and with a corresponding ‘valid’ status in WFO, taxa that are available in CAT database. Accessions that have a value in the Lifeform field. * Exclusion: Taxa that are cultivars of are missing species information, Nursery and Nitobe material for ease of mapping, Accession whose lifeform is not included in this list: * woody_list = [‘Tree’, ‘Shrub’, ‘Shrub or Tree’] * herb_list = [‘Herbaceous Perennial’, ‘Climber_Liana_Vine’]. * Validation: Taxa names were cross-referenced against [WFO Taxonomic Backbone] to resolve synonyms.

3. Climate Rating Trends within the UBCBG Collection data
This section identifies Family and Genera that exhibit an “average” drop in growing suitability within its members.
NOTE: The driver of a plant’s “suitability” can be varied. In the case of CAT data, the most important driver is considered to be temperature.

Lack of temperature can be as significant as too much heat.
Botanical gardens often deal with plants that are outside their natural temperature envelope.
Collection taxa seen as “less adapted” by the Climate Assessment Tool under current conditions reflect “zone stretching”: planting into warmer microclimates in the garden.
Long-term climate misalignment for plants is often due to heat, not cold weather.

Mapping Technique To accurately visualize the density of the collection on a limited screen: * Jittering: We applied a randomized spatial offset of ~6 meters to mass plantings (e.g., Hosta beds) and shared coordinates. This “explodes” dense clusters to reveal individual plants without distorting their true location. * Layers: Points are layered by LifeForm, allowing independent assessment of the canopy (Trees) vs. the understory (Perennials).

title: UBC Botanical Garden Climate Adaptation Analysis
text:
The Climate Assessment Tool (CAT) provided by Botanical Gardens Conservation Internation (BGCI) analysis provides a method to assessment of the UBC Botanical Garden’s collection against projected climate shifts. By integrating historical growth records from >3600 institutions from across the world, with localized climate modeling, the BGCI’s CAT tool attempts to describe a plants abilituy to adapt to a theoretical future ‘climate envelope’. This project uses the CAT data provided by the BGCI, along with UBCBG Garden Collection data andf Taxonomic data from World Flora Online to attempt identify risks, opportunities, and strategic priorities for curatorial management.
View Data Sources & Methodology


The analysis covers 82.2% of the documented collection, revealing distinct trends in survivability:

The 2050 Tipping Point: While many woody taxa remain resilient through 2050, herbaceous perennials show earlier signs of stress.
Spatial Vulnerability: Risk is not evenly distributed. The Asian Garden and Alpine sections face higher cumulative stress than the Carolinian Forest.







Exploratory Analysis Deep dive into the data coverage, family-level risks, and the “Climate Heroes” of the collection.



Interactive Risk Map Explore the garden spatially. Toggle between 2050 and 2090 scenarios to see the “heat sink” effect on specific beds.

title: Data Sources & Methodology
text:
This analysis synthesizes data from three primary sources to assess the climate resiliency of the living collection.



Source: UBC Botanical Garden IrisBG Database (Accession Item Report)
Scope: All currently living taxa in the Garden Collection, plus historically grown taxa for reference.
Taxonomy: Standardized using the World Flora Online (WFO) backbone.





Source: World Flora Online (WFO)
Scope: Current accepted taxonomy (as of December 2025) for all extant land plants worldwide, including synonym resolution.
Note: Future versions of this pipeline will utilize the WFO’s R package WorldFlora for automated name matching. The current method for deriving taxonomic statistics is detailed on the Validation Page.





Source: BGCI Climate Assessment Tool (CAT) Version 2.0 (Beta).
Analyst: Peter Symes (Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria / BGCI).

title: Data Sources & Methodology
text:
2. Climate Assessment Methodology

The “CAT” Tool: Version 1 vs. Version 2
While the Climate Assessment Tool (CAT) provided by BGCI is the industry standard for selecting climate-appropriate trees, the public version (V1) yielded insufficient coverage for our diverse collection.

Version Used: CAT Version 2.0 (Beta)
Coverage: 82.2% of the collection (compared to ~50% with V1)

Why Version 2? Initial trials with the public-facing CAT V1 resulted in low taxonomic matching (~50%) and flagged errors in the 2090 + Heat Island scenario. We collaborated with BGCI partners to run our dataset through the non-public CAT V2, which utilizes an expanded GlobalTreeSearch backbone and refined climate layers.


Data “Annealing” & Infraspecific Taxa
The integration of collection data with climate models followed a multi-stage “Annealing” process to maximize taxonomic coverage. To interface with the CAT algorithms, the collection data was normalized to the Species level.

Normalization: All infraspecific taxa (subspecies, varieties, cultivars) were rolled up to their parent Genus species.
Analysis: The unique list of species was analyzed in CAT V2.
Re-Annealing: The resulting climate ratings were mapped back to the original accession list using the species name as the key.

Limitation Note: This approach assumes that infraspecific taxa share the climate tolerance of the parent species. Consequently, a specific cultivar (e.g., Acer palmatum ‘Osakazuki’) inherits the broad climate rating of the species (Acer palmatum).

title: Data Sources & Methodology
text:
3. The “Climate Suitability” Metric
The analysis utilizes the Suitability Score (0-11) generated by CAT V2.

Definition: The score represents the consensus of climate models predicting suitability for a given taxon. A score of 11 indicates high confidence in suitability (match across all models/parameters), while 0 indicates a total mismatch.

Interpretation: * Score 9-11: High Suitability (Resilient) – The taxon is well-adapted to the projected climate conditions. * Score 5-8: Marginal Suitability (Moderate Risk) – The taxon may experience stress but is likely to survive with intervention. * Score 0-4: Low Suitability (High Risk/Vulnerable) – The taxon is poorly adapted and faces a high probability of failure without significant microclimate modification.

3. Observation record encoding
The observation records that are used to extrapolate range in the CAT model are based on a pooling data from several plant database (Plant Search, GBIF, GBIG-BGCI, Urban Plants). The number of observations in the given database has been entered as a string value “MODEL=#” where MODEL= is the model name and # is the number of observations. Three of the sheets from the CAT report had 5 columns with observation reports, while the fourth has only three observation columns after removing 2 erred columns earlier in this analysis. This data structure is untidy.
To tidy the data well apply a form of ‘one-hot coding’ whereby the model name becomes a unique column and the number of observation are recorded in the field when the model was used. This style preserves the boolean nature of one-hot, as any value other than nan/0 would be TRUE that that model was used in the analysis, all the while preserving the numerical value of the count
